topic: Mutual Fund and ETF Fees and Expenses
subtopic: Redemption, Exchange, Account, and Purchase Fees
source_evidence:
A no-load mutual fund is permitted to charge purchase fees, redemption fees, exchange fees, and account fees, none of which are considered sales loads.
If charged, you pay this fee when you redeem your shares (that is, sell your shares back to the mutual fund).
Some mutual funds may charge this fee if you exchange your shares in one mutual fund for shares of another mutual fund within the same mutual fund family.
This fee helps pay for the maintenance of your accounts.
Unlike a front-end sales load, which is paid to a selling broker, a purchase fee is paid to the mutual fund.
answer: Mutual funds may charge several shareholder fees for particular transactions or account maintenance, and a no-load fund can still have these fees. A redemption fee is charged when you sell shares back to the fund; it is paid to the fund and typically comes out of the money you receive. An exchange fee may apply when you switch from one fund to another within the same fund family. An account fee helps cover account maintenance and may, for example, apply to accounts below a specified value. A purchase fee is charged when you buy shares and goes to the mutual fund. It differs from a front-end sales load, which compensates the selling broker. Check the prospectus fee table to see which fees apply to a fund.
